cards.front: Where is most of the body's iron, and where is the stored fraction kept?
cards.back: An adult carries about 3.5 g of iron. Roughly 62% is in haemoglobin and about 25% is stored as ferritin and haemosiderin, mainly in reticuloendothelial cells in liver, spleen and marrow. The rest is in myoglobin and iron-containing enzymes.

cards.front: Compare the absorption of haeme iron with that of inorganic dietary iron.
cards.back: Haeme iron is absorbed best (up to about 35%) through a haeme carrier protein, without needing to be freed from its complex first. Inorganic iron averages about 5%: it must be reduced to the ferrous form, then enters the enterocyte through DMT1 and leaves the cell through ferroportin.

cards.front: Which substances impair the absorption of non-haeme iron, and which help it?
cards.back: Impairing: antacids and other alkalis (keep iron insoluble and block its reduction), phytates in cereals, phosphates, tetracyclines (chelation), and a heavy mixed meal in the stomach. Helping: gastric acid, reducing agents such as ascorbic acid and sulfhydryl amino acids, and meat, which adds haeme iron and stimulates acid.

cards.front: What is the mucosal block (ferritin curtain) and when is it overcome?
cards.back: Iron entering the enterocyte can be trapped as ferritin, which is lost when the cell is shed after 2 to 4 days. This limits absorption. The block is weakened in iron deficiency or brisk erythropoiesis, when more iron passes into plasma, and is overwhelmed by a gross excess of iron.

cards.front: What oral elemental iron dose gives the maximal haemopoietic response, and what is the prophylactic dose?
cards.back: KDT: about 200 mg of elemental iron a day in three divided doses gives the maximal haemopoietic response; about 30 mg a day is prophylactic. GG14 adds that a single dose of about 65 mg elemental iron (one 325 mg ferrous sulfate tablet) every other day maximises the fraction absorbed. Doses are always counted as elemental iron, not salt weight.

cards.front: When is parenteral iron indicated instead of oral iron?
cards.back: When oral iron is not tolerated, when it is not absorbed (malabsorption, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic inflammation), when the patient does not take it, in severe deficiency with ongoing blood loss, and in chronic kidney disease patients on erythropoietin who need iron faster than oral intake can supply.

cards.front: Iron dextran: what makes it unusual, and what are its main risks?
cards.back: It is the only iron preparation that can be given both i.m. and i.v. About 25% extra is added to the calculated dose because some stays locally bound at the injection site. It has the highest rate of hypersensitivity, including anaphylactoid collapse, because dextran is antigenic. A test dose is no longer recommended, and resuscitation facilities must be ready before any i.v. dose.

cards.front: Which newer intravenous iron products are the most convenient and safest, and why?
cards.back: Ferric carboxymaltose and iron isomaltoside 1000 are considered the two most convenient and safest i.v. options. Ferric carboxymaltose can be given as a single infusion of up to 1000 mg in saline (not glucose) and must not be given i.m. Iron isomaltoside 1000 allows a single 1 to 2 g infusion over 15 to 30 minutes, because its tight matrix releases little labile iron.

cards.front: Which drug is the chelator of choice in acute iron poisoning, and why is dimercaprol (BAL) avoided?
cards.back: Desferrioxamine (deferoxamine). It is given when plasma iron exceeds the total iron-binding capacity, and the IV route is used to chelate iron already absorbed; early chelation has cut the mortality of iron poisoning sharply. BAL (dimercaprol) is avoided because its iron complex is itself toxic.

cards.front: Short note: Acute iron poisoning

points: Mainly infants and children; about 10 to 20 tablets (over about 60 mg/kg elemental iron) can be serious
Very rare in adults
Vomiting, abdominal pain, haematemesis and bloody diarrhoea, then shock and lethargy
An apparent lull may be followed by severe metabolic acidosis, coma and death
Gut haemorrhage and necrosis; hepatic necrosis
Iron tablets are radiopaque, so an abdominal X-ray shows pills left in the gut
Whole bowel irrigation flushes out unabsorbed tablets
Activated charcoal does not adsorb iron
Desferrioxamine IV when plasma iron exceeds total iron-binding capacity
Speed matters: early treatment cuts mortality from about 45% to about 1%
DTPA or calcium edetate if desferrioxamine is unavailable; BAL is contraindicated
Correct fluid, electrolyte and acid-base disturbance
Support respiration and blood pressure; control convulsions

cards.front: Short note: Oral iron preparations - choice, dosing and adverse effects

points: Dissociable ferrous salts are cheap, high in iron and better absorbed than ferric forms
Ferrous sulfate is the standard cheapest choice
Ferrous gluconate and ferrous fumarate are alternatives
Carbonyl iron is fine metallic iron with about three-quarters of the bioavailability of ferrous sulfate
About 200 mg elemental iron a day in three divided doses for the maximal response
Prophylaxis about 30 mg daily
Sustained-release forms are not rational, since most iron is absorbed in the upper gut
Empty stomach improves absorption but increases side effects
Liquid preparations can stain teeth; place them at the back of the tongue
Epigastric pain, nausea, bloating, metallic taste, colic; constipation is more common than diarrhoea
Dose-related; start low and build up to improve tolerance
Multi-vitamin iron products are no better than plain ferrous salts; the Indian advisory board recommends no B-complex vitamins or zinc in haematinics

cards.front: Short note: Erythropoietin - actions and use in chronic kidney disease

points: Sialoglycoprotein of about 34,000 MW, made mainly by renal peritubular cells
Released in response to anaemia or hypoxia
Acts through a JAK-STAT-linked receptor to expand erythroid progenitors, speed haemoglobin synthesis and release reticulocytes
Epoetin: recombinant, given IV or s.c.; plasma half-life 6 to 10 h but the effect lasts several days
Darbepoetin: longer acting (half-life 24 to 36 h), given weekly
Anaemia of chronic renal failure
Do not push haemoglobin above about 11 g/dl: higher targets raised cardiovascular events, stroke, thrombosis and deaths
Also chemotherapy-induced anaemia (used conservatively), zidovudine-related anaemia and pre-operative autologous donation
Poor response in nutritional anaemia and primary marrow disease
Hypertension and thrombotic complications, including clotting of AV shunts
Most patients need concurrent iron
Rarely pure red cell aplasia from neutralising anti-erythropoietin antibodies, mainly with long-term s.c. use in dialysis patients

cards.front: Short note: Methotrexate toxicity and folinic acid rescue

points: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, depleting reduced folate coenzymes
Folinic acid (leucovorin, 5-formyl THF) is already reduced and bypasses the blocked enzyme
Folinic acid counteracts methotrexate toxicity; folic acid does not
KDT gives 3 mg IV, repeated as required
Large-dose methotrexate infusions are given only when leucovorin rescue follows within 24 h of the infusion
If the methotrexate level at 48 h is still 1 µM or more, higher leucovorin doses are continued until it falls below 50 nM
Hydration and urinary alkalinisation reduce methotrexate nephrotoxicity
Given with 5-fluorouracil to enhance its effect on thymidylate synthase
Expensive; plain folic acid is enough for simple folate deficiency

cards.front: Essay: Iron - absorption, storage and therapy of iron deficiency

points: Total body iron about 3.5 g; more in men than in women
Haemoglobin holds most of it; ferritin and haemosiderin hold the stores
Daily loss about 0.5 to 1 mg; higher needs in menstruating women, pregnancy (last two trimesters) and infancy
Haeme iron absorbed up to about 35%; inorganic iron about 5%
Enhanced by acid and reducing agents; impaired by antacids, phytates, phosphates and tetracyclines
Transported across the enterocyte by DMT1 and ferroportin; the mucosal block limits entry of excess
Plasma iron is bound to transferrin and enters cells through transferrin receptors
Erythroid cells express more receptors in iron deficiency and haemolysis
Stored as ferritin in reticuloendothelial cells, liver and marrow
Preferred route; ferrous salts, about 200 mg elemental iron a day
Side effects are dose-related
Haemoglobin rises about 0.5 to 1 g/dl per week; continue for 2 to 3 months after normalisation to replenish stores
Indicated when oral iron fails or is not tolerated, in malabsorption, non-compliance, chronic blood loss, or CKD on erythropoietin
Options: iron dextran, ferrous sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose, iron isomaltoside 1000
Monitor for hypersensitivity; have resuscitation ready for i.v. iron
Prophylaxis in late pregnancy, menorrhagia, infancy and chronic illness
Acute poisoning needs early gut decontamination and desferrioxamine

cards.front: Essay: Megaloblastic anaemia - vitamin B12 and folic acid

points: Deficiency of B12 or folate causes megaloblastic anaemia: large precursors in marrow and large, short-lived red cells
Basic defect is impaired DNA synthesis
Hypersegmented neutrophils and giant platelets are seen
Active coenzymes: methylcobalamin (methionine synthesis) and deoxyadenosylcobalamin (methylmalonyl-CoA pathway)
In deficiency, folate is trapped in the methyl form, so thymidylate synthesis fails
Absorbed with intrinsic factor from the stomach, mainly in the ileum; liver stores 2 to 8 mg, with enterohepatic recycling
Causes: pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor), gastric disease, malabsorption, blind-loop syndrome, fish tapeworm, strict vegetarian diet
Neurological damage: subacute combined degeneration, peripheral neuropathy

Hydroxocobalamin is preferred (more protein bound, stays longer): 100 to 1000 µg i.m. daily or alternate days for 1 to 2 weeks, then monthly for life; every 1 to 2 weeks for 6 months first if neurological signs are present
Oral B12 with intrinsic factor is unreliable, but 1000 µg oral B12 daily is usually sufficient even in pernicious anaemia
Haematological response within days to weeks; neurological recovery is slow
Causes: poor intake, malabsorption, alcohol, pregnancy, haemolysis, phenytoin, phenobarbitone and oral contraceptives
Stores last only 3 to 4 months
Treatment: oral folic acid 2 to 5 mg a day
Neural tube defect prevention: at least 400 µg a day from a month before conception through the first trimester
Never give folic acid alone to a patient with B12 deficiency: the blood improves but neurological damage can worsen
Folate deficiency alone does not cause neurological signs

cards.front: Classify: oral iron preparations
cards.text: Dissociable oral salts include {{ferrous sulfate}}, {{ferrous fumarate}} and {{ferrous gluconate}}; {{carbonyl iron}} is a fine metallic powder with about three-quarters the bioavailability of ferrous sulfate.

cards.front: Classify: intravenous iron products
cards.text: Iron {{dextran}} can be given both i.m. and i.v.; {{ferrous sucrose}} is given only i.v., with a single dose of up to {{200 mg}}; {{ferric carboxymaltose}} and {{iron isomaltoside 1000}} allow large single infusions.

cards.front: Classify: maturation factors
cards.text: Vitamin B12 is absorbed only when bound to {{intrinsic factor}} made in the {{stomach}}; folate is absorbed mainly in the {{upper intestine}}; the body's folate stores last only {{3 to 4 months}} without a supply.

cards.front: Which clotting tests explore the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, and what does each test?
cards.back: The aPTT explores the intrinsic (contact-activation) pathway and the common pathway. The prothrombin time (PT) explores the extrinsic (tissue factor) pathway and the common pathway. The extrinsic route activates factor X within seconds; the intrinsic route is slow and takes minutes.

cards.front: How does vitamin K take part in blood clotting?
cards.back: Vitamin K is a cofactor for the hepatic enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which adds carboxyl groups to glutamate residues of factors II, VII, IX and X. This lets them bind calcium and phospholipid surfaces. Protein C, protein S and osteocalcin use the same step.

cards.front: How do coumarin anticoagulants block clotting?
cards.back: They inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), so reduced vitamin K cannot be regenerated. The liver then makes under-carboxylated, inactive factors II, VII, IX and X. Coumarins work only in vivo and act with a delay of 1 to 3 days, because already-circulating factors must decay.

cards.front: On warfarin, which clotting factor falls first, and why does the effect take days to appear?
cards.back: Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 h), so it falls first, followed by factor IX (about 24 h), factor X (about 40 h) and prothrombin (about 60 h). Synthesis slows within hours, but the full effect appears over 1 to 3 days as circulating factors decline. A larger loading dose only slightly hastens it.

cards.front: Which drugs and conditions increase the effect of warfarin, and by what mechanism?
cards.back: Broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce gut vitamin K production; ceftriaxone and cefoperazone add a direct hypoprothrombinaemic effect; aspirin adds platelet inhibition and GI bleeding; sulfonamides, phenytoin and indomethacin displace warfarin from albumin; chloramphenicol, erythromycin, metronidazole, amiodarone, cimetidine and allopurinol inhibit its metabolism. Liver disease, malnutrition and hyperthyroidism also increase the effect.

cards.front: Which drugs reduce the effect of warfarin, and why is stopping them dangerous?
cards.back: Barbiturates (not benzodiazepines), carbamazepine, rifampicin and griseofulvin induce warfarin metabolism; oral contraceptives raise clotting factor levels. If an inducer is withdrawn while warfarin continues, the INR can rise sharply, and fatal bleeding has occurred.

cards.front: What INR ranges are used for warfarin therapy?
cards.back: INR 2 to 3 for most indications, such as venous thromboembolism and atrial fibrillation. A higher range of 2.5 to 3.5 is used for mechanical heart valves in the mitral position, or mechanical valves in another position with atrial fibrillation or a prior stroke. Intracranial bleeding risk rises steeply above INR 4. The INR corrects the prothrombin time for the sensitivity of the thromboplastin used, so results are comparable between laboratories.

cards.front: How is excess anticoagulation or bleeding on warfarin managed?
cards.back: No bleeding, raised INR: hold warfarin and restart at a lower dose once the INR is in range; if the INR is 10 or more, give oral vitamin K1 2.5 to 5 mg, which lowers the INR within 24 to 48 h without causing warfarin resistance. Serious bleeding: four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K1 10 mg by slow IV infusion (IV vitamin K can cause anaphylactoid reactions). Vitamin K acts slowly because factors must be resynthesised, and high doses make the patient unresponsive to warfarin for several days.

cards.front: How does heparin produce anticoagulation?
cards.back: Heparin binds antithrombin III and greatly speeds its inhibition of factors Xa, IIa (thrombin), IXa, XIa and XIIa, but not VIIa. Its long chain also acts as a scaffold that brings thrombin and antithrombin together. The effect is immediate in vivo and in vitro.

cards.front: Why does low-concentration heparin prolong aPTT more than PT?
cards.back: At low concentration heparin mainly blocks factor Xa-driven thrombin generation, which amplifies the intrinsic pathway, so aPTT rises while PT barely changes. At high concentration it also blocks the common pathway, and PT is prolonged.

cards.front: What is the standard i.v. heparin regimen and the monitoring target?
cards.back: Continuous IV infusion after a bolus: GG14 gives a 5000 U fixed or weight-adjusted bolus, then 800 to 1600 U/h (KDT: 5000 to 10000 U bolus, then 750 to 1000 U/h). Titrate to an aPTT of 1.5 to 2.5 times control (about 50 to 80 s). Intermittent IV bolus dosing is no longer recommended.

cards.front: How is heparin reversed with protamine, and what are its limits and dangers?
cards.back: Protamine, a basic protein, neutralises heparin about 1 mg per 100 U. It does not reverse fondaparinux and only partly reverses low molecular weight heparins. Inject it slowly (about 5 mg/min); rapid injection causes flushing and breathlessness. It can itself act as an anticoagulant and can cause hypersensitivity.

cards.front: What is danaparoid, and when is it used?
cards.back: A heparinoid preparation consisting mainly of heparan sulfate from pig gut mucosa. Its anticoagulant action is weaker than heparin's. It is used in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

cards.front: How does aspirin inhibit platelets, and why does its effect last for days?
cards.back: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, which stops thromboxane A2 synthesis. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts until new platelets are formed; bleeding time stays prolonged for 5 to 7 days. Low daily doses accumulate. Daily doses of 100 mg or less are used for most indications; higher doses also inhibit vascular prostacyclin and add bleeding without extra benefit.

cards.front: Dabigatran: how is it given, and how is it reversed?
cards.back: Dabigatran etexilate is an oral prodrug converted to dabigatran, a reversible direct thrombin inhibitor. About 80% of absorbed drug is excreted unchanged by the kidney, so the dose is reduced in severe renal impairment. It has no CYP3A4 interaction, but it is a P-glycoprotein substrate. Idarucizumab, a humanised antibody fragment, is the specific reversal agent. It must not be used with mechanical heart valves or triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome.

cards.front: Short note: Unfractionated heparin vs low molecular weight heparin vs fondaparinux

points: UFH: binds antithrombin III and needs a long chain to inhibit both Xa and IIa
LMWH: mainly anti-Xa, little thrombin inhibition
Fondaparinux: synthetic pentasaccharide, selectively inhibits Xa through antithrombin
UFH: poor and variable s.c. bioavailability, dose-dependent half-life
LMWH: good s.c. bioavailability, half-life 4 to 6 h, once- or twice-daily dosing
Fondaparinux: half-life 17 h, excreted in urine
UFH needs aPTT monitoring; LMWH and fondaparinux usually need none (anti-Xa assay in renal impairment, obesity, pregnancy, children)
Protamine fully reverses UFH, partly reverses LMWH and does not reverse fondaparinux
LMWH and fondaparinux cause less HIT than UFH
LMWH and fondaparinux are renally cleared and contraindicated if creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min; UFH is used in severe renal failure
UFH: cardiopulmonary bypass, catheter patency and when rapid reversal may be needed
LMWH and fondaparinux: DVT and PE prophylaxis and treatment, unstable angina and MI
Pregnancy: heparin, LMWH and fondaparinux do not cross the placenta and are the anticoagulants of choice

cards.front: Short note: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

points: IgG antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes activate platelets
Platelet count below 150,000/µL or a 50% fall, typically 5 to 10 days after starting heparin
Less common with LMWH and rare with fondaparinux
Paradoxical thrombosis: venous thromboembolism most often, also limb arterial occlusion, MI or stroke
Thrombosis may precede the fall in platelets; limb amputation in severe cases
Other features: adrenal haemorrhage, skin lesions at injection sites
Suspect when platelets fall 5 or more days after starting heparin
Confirm with an immunoassay for heparin-PF4 antibodies or a heparin-dependent platelet activation assay
Stop all heparin immediately; LMWH cross-reacts and must be avoided
Give an alternative anticoagulant because thrombosis can follow stopping heparin: argatroban (liver-cleared, usable in renal disease), bivalirudin or rivaroxaban; fondaparinux is another option
Do not start warfarin until the platelet count recovers: it can cause venous limb gangrene or skin necrosis
Bivalirudin or argatroban replaces heparin for PCI in patients with or at risk of HIT

cards.front: Short note: Warfarin vs direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs)

points: Vitamin K antagonist; onset over days; narrow therapeutic range
Needs INR monitoring and has many interactions
Reversal: vitamin K1 and four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
Rivaroxaban: 10 mg once daily for prophylaxis after knee or hip replacement; VTE treatment 15 mg twice daily for 21 days, then 20 mg daily; half-life 7 to 11 h
Apixaban: half-life about 12 h; AF 5 mg twice daily (2.5 mg if two of: age 80 or more, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or more); VTE 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily
Rivaroxaban and apixaban are CYP3A4 and P-gp substrates; edoxaban has minimal CYP3A4 metabolism
Dabigatran: prodrug, about 80% renal excretion; 150 mg twice daily in atrial fibrillation
Major bleeding similar to warfarin but about 70% less intracranial bleeding; more GI bleeding and dyspepsia
Lower once-daily doses are licensed in some countries for prophylaxis after hip or knee arthroplasty
Rapid onset and offset, fixed dosing, no routine monitoring, fewer interactions
Comparable or better than warfarin for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF
Avoid with mechanical heart valves and triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran
Andexanet alfa (recombinant inactive factor Xa decoy) reverses rivaroxaban and apixaban in serious bleeding
Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate if andexanet is unavailable

cards.front: Short note: P2Y12 inhibitors - clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor

points: Thienopyridine prodrug, activated in the liver mainly by CYP2C19
Irreversible P2Y12 blockade; platelet recovery takes about 5 days
Slow and variable response: CYP2C19 polymorphism; proton pump inhibitors that inhibit CYP2C19 may reduce activation
Loading 300 mg (600 mg before PCI), then 75 mg daily; bleeding is the main adverse effect
Faster, more complete activation; less affected by CYP2C19 variation and omeprazole
Irreversible; platelet recovery takes about 7 days
Loading 60 mg, then 10 mg daily (5 mg if under 60 kg)
More serious bleeding than clopidogrel; contraindicated after prior stroke or TIA; not for patients over 75
Active drug, no metabolic activation; reversible P2Y12 blocker with faster onset and offset
Half-life about 12 h, twice-daily dosing; loading dose 180 mg
Dyspnoea in about 17%; more intracranial bleeding than clopidogrel
Aspirin above 100 mg a day reduces its effect; metabolised by CYP3A4
Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor) for ACS and after stenting

cards.front: Short note: Fibrinolytic (thrombolytic) drugs

points: Convert plasminogen to plasmin, which digests fibrin
Work best on fresh venous thrombi; little effect on thrombi older than 3 days
Main hazard is bleeding, since plasmin also degrades clotting factors
Streptokinase: not fibrin-specific, antigenic, cannot be reused, anaphylaxis in 1 to 2%
Alteplase: fibrin-selective, half-life 4 to 8 min, infused over about 90 min for MI with heparin and aspirin
Reteplase: deletion mutant, given as two boluses 30 min apart
Tenecteplase: fibrin-selective, longer acting, resistant to PAI-1, given as a single bolus
STEMI as an alternative to primary PCI; benefit is greatest in the first hour
Ischaemic stroke: alteplase within 3 to 4.5 h when contraindications are excluded
Large life-threatening PE; DVT; limb arterial occlusion when surgery is not possible
Previous intracranial haemorrhage, recent ischaemic stroke or head injury, active bleeding, anticoagulation, recent major surgery, uncontrolled hypertension, pregnancy

cards.front: Short note: Tranexamic acid and aminocaproic acid (EACA)

points: Lysine analogues that block the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen and plasmin, preventing fibrin binding
Tranexamic acid is about 7 times more potent than EACA
Oral or IV; IV loading 4 to 5 g over 1 h, then 1 to 1.25 g/h; no more than 30 g in 24 h
Rapid IV injection causes hypotension, bradycardia and arrhythmia; rarely myopathy; intravascular thrombosis
Renally excreted; use cautiously in renal impairment
Bleeding from fibrinolytics, cardiopulmonary bypass and other cardiac surgery, hip or knee arthroplasty
Tonsillectomy, prostatectomy, dental extraction in haemophilia, menorrhagia, recurrent epistaxis
Given IV in trauma resuscitation, massive haemorrhage and postpartum haemorrhage
Nausea and diarrhoea are the main effects
Thromboembolism, colour vision disturbance and allergy are infrequent; thrombophlebitis at the injected vein

cards.front: Essay: Anticoagulants - classification, mechanism and clinical choice

points: Anticoagulants reduce fibrin formation and prevent thrombus extension; they do not dissolve existing clot
Most effective in venous thrombosis, which is fibrin-rich
Antiplatelet drugs are preferred in arterial disease
UFH: acts through antithrombin III; aPTT monitoring; protamine reversal
LMWH and fondaparinux: s.c., predictable, mainly anti-Xa, renal clearance
Bivalirudin and argatroban: direct thrombin inhibitors used in HIT and PCI
Blocks VKOR, reducing vitamin K-dependent factors; INR monitoring; delayed onset
Many interactions; contraindicated in pregnancy (birth defects)
Reversal: vitamin K1 and prothrombin complex concentrate
Rivaroxaban, apixaban and edoxaban inhibit factor Xa; dabigatran inhibits thrombin
Fixed dosing without routine monitoring
Reversal: idarucizumab for dabigatran; andexanet alfa for rivaroxaban and apixaban
VTE prophylaxis after knee or hip replacement: LMWH, low-dose UFH, fondaparinux or a DOAC
Acute VTE: parenteral agent overlapped with warfarin for at least 5 days, or rivaroxaban or apixaban alone from the start
Stroke prevention in non-valvular AF: DOAC or warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated with mechanical heart valves
Pregnancy: heparin or LMWH
Bleeding is the chief hazard; HIT; osteoporosis with long-term high-dose UFH
Contraindications: bleeding disorders, severe hypertension, threatened abortion, peptic ulcer, endocarditis, ocular or neurosurgery, lumbar puncture

cards.front: Essay: Antiplatelet drugs in acute coronary syndrome

points: Platelet adhesion to von Willebrand factor and collagen; release of thromboxane A2 and ADP
GPIIb/IIIa binding fibrinogen cross-links platelets into a plug
Platelets dominate arterial thrombi, so antiplatelets suit arterial disease
Irreversible COX-1 acetylation blocks thromboxane A2
Low doses (100 mg a day or less) for long-term use
Clopidogrel, prasugrel and ticagrelor, given with aspirin
Prasugrel or ticagrelor act faster and more predictably than clopidogrel and are commonly chosen for PCI
Ticagrelor is reversible; avoid aspirin above 100 mg a day with it
Abciximab, eptifibatide and tirofiban block the final common pathway of aggregation
Used with aspirin and heparin during high-risk PCI for a limited infusion period
Main risks: bleeding and thrombocytopenia
Phosphodiesterase inhibitor and adenosine uptake blocker that raises platelet cAMP
Added to low-dose aspirin for secondary stroke prevention (ESPS-2)
Unstable angina and NSTEMI: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor
STEMI: primary PCI within 12 h with prasugrel or ticagrelor plus aspirin; dual therapy after stenting
Stroke and TIA: aspirin or clopidogrel; short-term dual therapy may help, but long-term dual therapy increases haemorrhage

cards.front: Essay: Drugs for bleeding - coagulants, vitamin K and haemostatics

points: Haemostasis: vessel spasm, platelet plug, coagulation and later fibrinolysis
Choose the drug by cause: factor deficiency, platelet defect, fibrinolysis or capillary bleeding
Fresh whole blood or fresh frozen plasma supplies all factors
Fibrinogen for afibrinogenaemia and bleeding in haemophilia
Factor VIII concentrate for haemophilia A: 5 to 10 U/kg, action lasts only 1 to 2 days
Treats dietary deficiency, obstructive jaundice, malabsorption, antibiotic-induced deficiency, and haemorrhagic disease of the newborn
Phytonadione i.m. or oral; the i.v. emulsion can cause anaphylactoid reactions
Menadione should not be used: it causes haemolysis and can precipitate kernicterus in neonates
Desmopressin releases factor VIII and von Willebrand factor from endothelium
Tranexamic acid and EACA control fibrinolysis-related bleeding
Local haemostatics: absorbable gelatin, oxidised cellulose, fibrin, topical thrombin, adrenaline-soaked packing for nasal bleeding
Ethamsylate, rutin and adrenochrome: efficacy unproven; ethamsylate is not recommended
Sclerosants (sodium tetradecyl sulfate, polidocanol) for varices and piles

cards.front: Classify: vitamin K-dependent proteins
cards.text: The vitamin K-dependent clotting factors are {{II}}, {{VII}}, {{IX}} and {{X}}; the anticoagulant proteins {{protein C}} and {{protein S}} are also vitamin K-dependent.

cards.front: Complete: metabolism of the warfarin enantiomers
cards.text: Warfarin is a racemate; the {{S}} enantiomer is 3 to 5 times more potent and is cleared mainly by {{CYP2C9}}, whose polymorphisms (with {{VKORC1}} variants) alter dose needs. KDT states the less potent R enantiomer is degraded by side-chain reduction through CYP1A and CYP3A4.

cards.front: Classify: vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants
cards.text: {{Warfarin}} has a half-life of {{36 to 48 h}}; {{acenocoumarol}} has an overall effective duration of about {{24 h}} through its active metabolite; {{ethyl biscoumacetate}} acts rapidly and briefly; {{bishydroxycoumarin}} is slowly and unpredictably absorbed.

cards.front: Classify: direct oral anticoagulants
cards.text: {{Rivaroxaban}} and {{apixaban}} inhibit {{factor Xa}}; {{dabigatran etexilate}}, a prodrug, is converted to a direct inhibitor of {{thrombin}}; dabigatran is mainly cleared by the {{kidney}} and is reversed by {{idarucizumab}}.

cards.front: Classify: fibrinolytic agents
cards.text: Fibrin-selective agents include {{alteplase}}, {{reteplase}} and {{tenecteplase}}; {{streptokinase}} is not fibrin-specific and is antigenic; {{urokinase}} has gone out of use.

cards.front: Classify: platelet inhibitors by target
cards.text: GP IIb/IIIa antagonists include {{abciximab}}, {{eptifibatide}} and {{tirofiban}}; the thienopyridines {{clopidogrel}} and {{prasugrel}} irreversibly block the {{P2Y12}} receptor; {{ticagrelor}} blocks the same receptor reversibly.

cards.front: What roles do chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL and HDL play in lipid transport?
cards.back: Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride from the gut. VLDL carries liver-made triglyceride. Its remnant, IDL, loses more triglyceride and becomes LDL, which carries cholesterol to tissues and liver. HDL removes excess cholesterol from tissues. Raised LDL and VLDL are atherogenic; HDL is protective.

cards.front: How do statins lower LDL cholesterol?
cards.back: They competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Hepatic cholesterol falls, which increases LDL receptor expression on liver cells, so more IDL and LDL are cleared from blood. Over the long term, feedback partly restores synthesis, leaving a dose-dependent lowering of LDL.

cards.front: Why are statins given at bedtime, and which statins are exceptions?
cards.back: Cholesterol synthesis by HMG-CoA reductase peaks around midnight, so statins are given at night for maximal effect. Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin have long half-lives and can be taken at any time of day.

cards.front: Statin myopathy: how common is it, and which drugs raise the risk?
cards.back: Muscle aches are common, but true myopathy is rare (under 1 in 1000) and rhabdomyolysis deaths are on record. Risk rises with gemfibrozil and nicotinic acid, and with CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides such as erythromycin, azole antifungals, cyclosporine, nefazodone, HIV protease inhibitors, amiodarone). Pravastatin, fluvastatin and rosuvastatin are not extensively metabolised by CYP3A4, so they carry less interaction risk. Simvastatin 80 mg is not advised; simvastatin should not exceed 20 mg with amlodipine or amiodarone, or 10 mg with diltiazem or verapamil.

cards.front: Which fibrate is preferred alongside a statin, and why should gemfibrozil be avoided with statins?
cards.back: Fenofibrate interferes least with statin handling, so it is preferred when a fibrate must be combined. Gemfibrozil blocks hepatic uptake of the active statin acids through the OATP1B1 transporter (called OATP2 in KDT) and competes for the glucuronidation that clears most statins, nearly doubling statin levels and raising the risk of myopathy; avoid the combination.

cards.front: How does ezetimibe lower LDL cholesterol, and what is its main role?
cards.back: It blocks NPC1L1, the intestinal transporter for dietary and biliary cholesterol and phytosterols, lowering LDL by about 15 to 20%. It is mainly an add-on to a statin, with a synergistic effect. Its extra outcome benefit is small, about 2% in IMPROVE-IT with simvastatin.

cards.front: Why are bile acid sequestrants seldom used, and what do they do to triglycerides?
cards.back: Cholestyramine, colestipol and colesevelam bind bile acids in the gut, which increases hepatic LDL receptor expression and lowers LDL by about 15 to 25%. Triglycerides are not lowered and may rise. They are seldom used because they are unpalatable, need large doses, cause flatulence and GI upset, bind other drugs, and are poorly accepted.

cards.front: How do fibrates work, and what lipid changes do they produce?
cards.back: They activate PPAR-alpha, which increases lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid oxidation and reduces hepatic triglyceride synthesis. Triglycerides fall by 20 to 50%, LDL falls by 5 to 15%, and HDL rises by 10 to 20%. Their main use is severe hypertriglyceridaemia.

cards.front: Why is nicotinic acid useful, and what limits its use?
cards.back: It is the most effective drug for raising HDL, and it also lowers triglycerides, LDL and lipoprotein(a). It inhibits adipocyte lipolysis and hepatic VLDL production. Flushing (mediated by prostaglandin D2) limits use; aspirin before a dose reduces it. Dyspepsia, hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia and liver damage are other limits, and doses above 2 g a day are poorly tolerated. Added to statins it gave no outcome benefit (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE), and in 2016 the FDA withdrew approval of extended-release niacin as statin add-on therapy.

cards.front: Short note: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins)

points: Competitive inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase; LDL-receptor upregulation
Dose-dependent LDL fall; modest fall in triglycerides and rise in HDL
Lovastatin and simvastatin: lipophilic lactone prodrugs with short half-lives
Lovastatin, simvastatin and atorvastatin rely on CYP3A4; pravastatin, fluvastatin and rosuvastatin are not extensively metabolised by CYP3A4
Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin have long half-lives and can be taken at any time; atorvastatin needs no dose change in severe renal dysfunction
Well tolerated; GI upset, headache, rise in transaminases
Serious liver injury is very rare; routine liver enzyme monitoring after starting is no longer recommended, only testing if symptoms suggest liver injury
Muscle aches common; myopathy rare; rhabdomyolysis can be fatal
Contraindicated in pregnancy; stop before conception if possible
Gemfibrozil and nicotinic acid increase myopathy risk
CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels of CYP3A4-dependent statins
First-choice drug for raised LDL, primary and secondary hypercholesterolaemia, and diabetic dyslipidaemia
Reduce ASCVD events and mortality; continued long term

cards.front: Short note: Management of hypertriglyceridaemia

points: Correct reversible causes: obesity, inactivity, high-carbohydrate or high-calorie diet, alcohol, smoking, diabetes, kidney disease, corticosteroids, oestrogens, high-dose beta-blockers, hypothyroidism
Statin therapy for LDL may itself lower triglycerides
Very high triglycerides are a major risk factor for acute pancreatitis
With triglycerides above 1000 mg/dl, a fibrate or fish oil is recommended to prevent pancreatitis
Fibrates: KDT lists gemfibrozil 600 mg twice daily as first line for markedly raised triglycerides; fenofibrate is preferred when a statin is also used
Omega-3 fatty acid ethyl esters 3 to 4 g a day with food for severe hypertriglyceridaemia
Icosapent ethyl (purified EPA) 4 g a day as an add-on to statins
Nicotinic acid is now little used
Fibrate or niacin added to a statin has not shown outcome benefit; the FDA withdrew these add-on approvals in 2016
Stop a fibrate after 2 months if triglycerides are not adequately lowered; watch for myopathy with a statin

cards.front: Short note: Statin intensity categories and who gets them

points: High (LDL fall about 50% or more): atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg; rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg
Moderate (LDL fall 30 to 49%): atorvastatin 10 to 20 mg; rosuvastatin 5 to 10 mg; simvastatin 20 to 40 mg; pravastatin 40 to 80 mg; lovastatin 40 to 80 mg; fluvastatin 80 mg; pitavastatin 1 to 4 mg
Low (under 30%): e.g. simvastatin 10 mg, pravastatin 10 to 20 mg, lovastatin 20 mg
Clinical ASCVD: high intensity (moderate if over 75)
LDL 190 mg/dl or higher: high intensity
Diabetes, age 40 to 75, LDL 70 to 189 mg/dl: at least moderate intensity
Age 40 to 75, LDL 70 to 189 mg/dl, 10-year risk 7.5% or more: moderate to high intensity
Targets are percentage LDL falls: about 50% for high risk (10-year risk 20% or more), 30 to 49% for intermediate risk
Low risk (under 5%): lifestyle only
Ezetimibe, then PCSK9 inhibitors, are add-ons in clinical ASCVD
NICE (UK) uses slightly different bands and thresholds

cards.front: Essay: Hyperlipidaemia - classification, targets and drug therapy

points: Lipoproteins: chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL and HDL
LDL carries cholesterol to tissues; uptake depends on LDL receptor expression
HDL removes cholesterol from tissues and is protective
Secondary: diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, alcoholism, drugs such as corticosteroids and oral contraceptives
Primary: monogenic (familial) or polygenic and multifactorial
Examples: familial hypercholesterolaemia (LDL receptor defect, type IIa); familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia (abnormal apoE, type III); hypertriglyceridaemia (type IV)
Older NCEP ATP III (2001): LDL goals by risk group, e.g. under 100 mg/dl for high risk
2018 AHA/ACC: statin intensity and percentage LDL fall by risk, rather than fixed goals
Risk factors: age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, low HDL, family history, obesity
Low saturated and trans fat diet, regular exercise, weight control, smoking cessation, limited alcohol
The base of all treatment, with or without drugs
Statins are first line for raised LDL
Ezetimibe adds about 20% LDL lowering or replaces a statin in intolerance; bempedoic acid is another oral add-on
PCSK9 inhibitors for clinical ASCVD or familial hypercholesterolaemia not controlled on maximal statin
Fibrates or omega-3 fatty acids for very high triglycerides; bile acid sequestrants are poorly accepted
Lipid profile to check response; watch for myopathy
Liver enzymes if symptoms suggest liver injury

cards.front: Essay: Hypolipidaemic drugs - classes, mechanisms and adverse effects

points: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors; increase LDL-receptor clearance
Adverse: myopathy, transaminase rise; interactions with gemfibrozil and CYP3A4 inhibitors
Cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam; bind bile acids; LDL fall up to about 25%
Adverse: GI effects, flatulence; bind co-administered drugs
PPAR-alpha activation; lipoprotein lipase activation; triglycerides fall 20 to 50%
Gemfibrozil, bezafibrate, fenofibrate; adverse effects: GI upset, myalgia, gallstones; rhabdomyolysis rare
Inhibits adipocyte lipolysis and VLDL production; the most effective HDL-raising drug
Adverse: flushing, dyspepsia, hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia, liver damage
Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1); LDL fall about 20%; complementary to statins
PCSK9 monoclonal antibodies (alirocumab, evolocumab), s.c. every 2 weeks or monthly: the most effective LDL-lowering drugs
Inclisiran: siRNA against PCSK9 mRNA, s.c. at start, 3 months, then every 6 months
Bempedoic acid: oral ATP-citrate lyase inhibitor; hyperuricaemia, gout, tendon rupture
Lomitapide (MTP inhibitor) and evinacumab (anti-ANGPTL3) for homozygous FH
Saroglitazar: dual PPAR-alpha and gamma agonist, approved only in India for diabetic dyslipidaemia

cards.front: Classify: lipoproteins by main lipid
cards.text: Chylomicrons carry mainly {{triglyceride}} from the diet; VLDL carries mainly {{triglyceride}} made in the liver; LDL carries mainly {{cholesteryl ester}}; HDL removes {{cholesterol}} from tissues.

cards.front: Classify: statins by efficacy
cards.text: Lovastatin, pravastatin and simvastatin are low-to-moderate efficacy; {{atorvastatin}} and {{rosuvastatin}} are high efficacy; {{pitavastatin}} is the most potent dose for dose, but its ceiling dose is {{4 mg}} per day.

cards.front: Classify: hypolipidaemic drugs by target
cards.text: Ezetimibe blocks {{NPC1L1}} in the intestine; {{cholestyramine}} binds {{bile acids}} in the gut; nicotinic acid reduces hepatic {{VLDL}} production; fibrates activate {{PPAR-alpha}}.

cards.front: Classify: statin intensity categories
cards.text: High-intensity statins are {{atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg}} and {{rosuvastatin 20 to 40 mg}}; {{simvastatin 20 to 40 mg}} is a moderate-intensity statin; {{simvastatin 80 mg}} carries a higher myopathy risk and is not advised.

cards.front: Short note: PCSK9 inhibitors

points: PCSK9 is a protease that binds hepatic LDL receptors and sends them for lysosomal degradation
Blocking it leaves more LDL receptors on the liver surface, so more LDL is cleared
Alirocumab and evolocumab: fully human monoclonal antibodies that bind free PCSK9; s.c. every 2 weeks or once monthly
Inclisiran: siRNA that blocks PCSK9 synthesis; s.c. at start, at 3 months, then every 6 months; LDL down about half at 6 months
Add-on to maximally tolerated statin (with or without ezetimibe) in clinical ASCVD needing more LDL lowering
Heterozygous and homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia
Antibodies reduce MI and stroke in ASCVD (FOURIER, ODYSSEY OUTCOMES); high cost limits use to very high-risk patients
Injection-site reactions (most common), nasopharyngitis and other infections
Possible small neurocognitive risk under study
No known drug interactions; avoid in pregnancy

cards.front: Bempedoic acid: mechanism, effect and adverse effects?
cards.back: An oral prodrug activated in the liver (by very long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 1) to bempedoic acid-CoA, which inhibits ATP-citrate lyase upstream of HMG-CoA reductase. Less hepatic cholesterol synthesis upregulates LDL receptors. Alone it lowers LDL by 15 to 25%; with ezetimibe about 30%. Given once daily, also as a fixed combination with ezetimibe. Adverse effects: hyperuricaemia and gout, tendon rupture, raised CK, creatinine and transaminases.

cards.front: Andexanet alfa: what is it and when is it used?
cards.back: A recombinant factor Xa analogue with its active-site serine replaced and its Gla domain removed, so it has no clotting activity. It acts as a decoy that binds circulating rivaroxaban or apixaban and rapidly reverses their anti-Xa effect. Given as an IV bolus then a 2 h infusion, for serious bleeding such as intracranial haemorrhage. It also reverses heparin and LMWH, so it is avoided before procedures that need heparin. It is costly; four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate is used if it is unavailable.

cards.front: Why does warfarin dose requirement vary so much between patients?
cards.back: Genetic variation in two genes. CYP2C9 variants alter metabolism of the more potent S-warfarin (pharmacokinetic effect). VKORC1 variants make the target enzyme more sensitive to inhibition (pharmacodynamic effect). About 10% of patients need less than 1.5 mg a day to reach INR 2 to 3, often because they carry these variants. Genotyping both genes can help choose the starting dose. Diet, interacting drugs and illness add further variation.

cards.front: Short note: Pleiotropic effects of statins

points: Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, so LDL receptors are upregulated
Main effect is a fall in LDL; small fall in triglycerides and rise in HDL
Statins block mevalonate products that lipidate membrane enzymes such as endothelial NO synthase
Better endothelial function through more NO
Less LDL oxidation
Suppress macrophage-mediated inflammation, stabilising plaques and reducing rupture
Benefit in raised cholesterol without known coronary disease partly ascribed to these effects
Rosuvastatin reduces venous thromboembolism after knee surgery
Some of these actions are undesirable

cards.front: Short note: Haemopoietic growth factors

points: Regulates red cell production
Used for anaemia of chronic renal failure, chemotherapy, zidovudine therapy, premature infants and autologous blood donation
Can cause hypertension, iron deficiency and raised blood viscosity
G-CSF (filgrastim, pegfilgrastim, lenograstim) stimulates neutrophil progenitors
Pegfilgrastim is pegylated and acts longer
Used to shorten chemotherapy-induced neutropenia and to harvest progenitor cells
GM-CSF is also a recombinant CSF
Recombinant thrombopoietin caused neutralising antibodies and prolonged thrombocytopenia
Eltrombopag (oral) and romiplostim (injected) activate thrombopoietin receptors
Approved for ITP that has not responded to other treatment such as splenectomy
G-CSF: bone pain, fever, myalgia, rash and GI upset

cards.front: Short note: Direct thrombin inhibitors

points: Bind thrombin directly, so no antithrombin III is needed
Used when heparin cannot be used, e.g. heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
Synthetic 20-amino-acid peptide based on hirudin
Anticoagulant in PCI for STEMI, with aspirin and/or clopidogrel or a GP IIb/IIIa inhibitor
Useful where HIT risk exists
Synthetic non-peptide that binds the thrombin catalytic site reversibly
Given IV as a bolus then infusion; short-lasting; prolongs aPTT
Used for thrombosis in HIT and for PCI in patients with HIT
Oral prodrug converted to a reversible direct thrombin inhibitor
About 80% is excreted by the kidney
Reversed by idarucizumab

cards.front: Short note: Drugs abused in sports

points: Athletes use epoetin to raise haemoglobin (blood doping)
Misuse has been linked to deaths of several athletes and is strongly discouraged
Athletes take androgens, usually secretly, so effects are poorly documented
Early abuse used 17-alkylated anabolic steroids, which were thought to be more anabolic than androgenic
Many of these compounds can be detected readily by testing

cards.front: Short note: Direct thrombin inhibitors

points: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: heparin must be stopped; low molecular weight heparins are not safe, so a direct thrombin inhibitor is used

cards.front: Short note: Erythropoietin (epoetin)

points: Recombinant human erythropoietin (epoetin alfa and beta), given i.v. or s.c.
Stimulates erythropoiesis in a dose-dependent manner
Has no effect on red cell lifespan
